Aviation works in UTC (also called Zulu or Z), the same time everywhere. Clients think in local time.

Flight time runs from take-off to landing. Block time runs from when the aircraft moves off its stand to when it stops at the destination. Operators price on either; their quote says which.
A positioning leg (also called a ferry) is a flight without passengers to bring the aircraft to the client, or back to base. The client usually pays for it.
An empty leg is a positioning flight the operator sells cheaply. It can be cancelled or moved if the main trip changes.
A one-way trip can cost almost as much as a return if the aircraft must fly back empty.

0.6 Permits, slots and border control
Permits: most countries require permission for a foreign commercial flight to land or fly over them.
Slots: busy airports allocate take-off and landing times. A permit may not be issued until a slot is confirmed.
PPR (prior permission required): some airports require advance approval for parking or for the flight.
Border control: passengers pass customs, immigration and health checks. Authorities may require passenger details in advance.
Lead times vary by country and airport, and change. The operator and its trip support know the current rules: we ask them every time.

text: Aviation for brokers
0.7 Crew duty

Pilots and cabin crew may only work a limited number of hours in a duty period, set by their authority. A long flight, an early start after a late arrival, or several legs in one day can exceed those limits. The operator then adds a second crew, flies a fresh crew in, or plans a night stop. This changes the price and the schedule, so we ask early.

0.12 The freedoms of the air
International agreements describe what an airline of one country may do in another country's airspace. They explain why some legs are allowed and others are not.

3rdhome to abroadHA5thon to a third countryHAB7thabroad onlyAB8ththrough-flight cabotageHAA9thstand-alone cabotageAAH operator's home countryA, B other countriesRed legs are domestic in aforeign country: cabotageThe 8th and 9th freedoms are cabotage, which most countries refuse to foreign operators.
1stFly over another country without landing
2ndLand in another country for a technical reason, such as fuel, without picking up or setting down passengers
3rdCarry passengers from your own country to another country
4thCarry passengers from another country back to your own country
5thCarry passengers between two foreign countries on a flight that starts or ends in your own country
6thCarry passengers between two foreign countries via your own country
7thCarry passengers between two foreign countries without touching your own country
8thCarry passengers between two points inside a foreign country on a flight that starts or ends in your own country (cabotage)
9thCarry passengers inside a foreign country on a stand-alone domestic flight (cabotage)

The 8th and 9th freedoms are cabotage, which most countries refuse to foreign operators (Module 2.4). Which freedoms an operator may use depends on agreements between countries and on the permits for each flight, so the operator always confirms.

For international flights between countries that have joined it, the Montreal Convention of 1999 sets what the air carrier (the operator) owes passengers for death or injury, delay and baggage. 1.8 The Archē portal: one place for everything

Every enquiry, quote, document, booking, payment record and commission for Archē lives in the Archē broker portal. Nothing is quoted, sold or paid outside it, and work done outside it earns no commission. The portal opens on your dashboard: your progress this month, your place in the team and every outstanding task, most urgent first.
Leads and prospects
The portal assigns organisations to brokers automatically and fairly: by country and region fit, follow-up record, conversions and fair share. Every active broker receives new leads every week.

Operations checks each trip, confirms the operator price on Avinode, completes KYC and sanctions screening, creates the payment request and issues the confirmation.

The operator and the captain decide how each of these is handled. The rules below explain why they exist, so you ask the right questions early and tell the client what may be charged.

De-icing and anti-icingNo take-off with frost, ice or snow on the wings, control surfaces, engines or sensors: EU CAT.OP.MPA.250 and US 14 CFR 135.227. Ground procedures follow ICAO Doc 9640 and SAE AS6285.Cold, wet weather: northern winter (about November to March), southern winter (about June to September), and high or cold airports at any timeList it as an operational need, charged at cost after the flight with the receipt. Allow extra time; never promise a departure time in icing conditions.

Airport hours and night restrictionsEach airport publishes its hours and restrictions in its country's aeronautical information publication (AIP) and in NOTAMs. Many have night curfews or noise rules.Late-night and early-morning departures or arrivalsAsk the operator whether the airport is open at that time. An out-of-hours opening may be possible at extra cost, or not at all: then change the time or the airport.

Slots and prior permission (PPR)Busy airports are slot-coordinated (in the EU under Regulation (EEC) No 95/93, elsewhere under national rules and the worldwide airport slot guidelines). Business aviation needs a slot there too. Some airports require prior permission for the flight or for parking.Major hubs, big events and peak seasonsThe operator or its trip support requests slots and PPR as soon as the trip is booked. Never promise a time before the slot is confirmed.

Customs, immigration and private terminalsAn international flight must land first at an airport with customs and immigration (Chicago Convention, Article 10). Authorities require passenger information in advance, for example eAPIS for the United States.Every international arrival and departureCheck that customs is available at the planned time. A private terminal (FBO or VIP terminal) can cost extra. Passenger details reach the operator by its deadline.

Crew duty and restLimits come from the operator's authority. Example: on US unscheduled Part 135 flights a two-pilot crew may fly up to 10 hours in 24 hours, within a duty period of up to 14 hours, with at least 10 hours of rest (14 CFR 135.267). In Europe, EU flight-time rules (ORO.FTL) apply to commercial operations, and national rules still apply to some business-jet air-taxi work.Long sectors, several legs in a day, an early start after a late arrivalAsk the operator for the crew plan in writing: extra crew, a fresh crew or a night stop. The cost is in the quote or listed as an operational need.

Crew hotel and allowancesCrew take their rest away from the aircraft.The aircraft waits with the client overnight or for several daysAgree with the operator whether hotel and allowances are in the price or charged at cost.

Parking and hangarageAirports limit parking space, and some require prior permission to park. A hangar protects the aircraft from snow and ice.Night stops and waiting days, especially at busy or winter airportsConfirm parking, or repositioning to another airport, before booking. A hangar in winter can avoid de-icing but costs extra.

Technical stops and long sectorsRange falls with load, headwinds and hot or high airports. Long flights over water can need ETOPS or EDTO approval (Module 6.3).Very long sectors and full cabinsOnly the operator confirms non-stop for that load and season. A technical stop adds time, fees and sometimes permits.

PermitsNon-scheduled flights need permission to land in, and often to fly over, other countries (Chicago Convention, Article 5, and national rules). Domestic legs on foreign aircraft are cabotage (Module 2).Every international trip; strictest in the countries in Appendix G.5Give the operator the full routing and passenger details at booking. Later changes need new permits and may be refused.

PetsEntry rules for animals differ by country (in the EU, Regulation (EU) No 576/2013). Some countries accept pets only on approved routes and at approved airports.Any animal on boardCheck the destination's rules and the operator's written acceptance before quoting. See Appendix G.4.

Dangerous goods and weaponsGoverned by ICAO Annex 18 and the ICAO Technical Instructions. Spare lithium batteries, oxygen, some medicines, firearms and ammunition are restricted.Any unusual item in the luggageAsk the client; the operator decides. Firearms and armed security need permits in every country involved: refer to the director.

Children and passengers needing helpInfants count as passengers on the manifest. Child seats must be acceptable to the operator. A passenger who needs medical care in flight needs an air ambulance.Families, elderly passengers, reduced mobilityList child seats and assistance as client requests. Medical care on board is never a normal charter: refer through the director.

Catering and allergiesThe caterer and the operator are responsible for food safety; they need allergies in writing.Every flight: always ask about allergiesWrite dietary needs and allergies on the order and get them confirmed back.

Anything that depends on the day (de-icing, extra parking, out-of-hours fees, crew nights after a change) is charged at cost after the flight, with receipts. Anything a supplier quotes in writing before booking can be a fixed price. Module 9.8 explains how each is priced.

8.3 Archē-approved operators

Many good operators, above all in Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, hold none of the audits in 8.2. The director can approve such an operator once, for twelve months, after the checks below. Approved operators are on the approved-operator list in the portal, with the date the approval ends, and brokers can quote them like an audited operator. The approval belongs to the AOC that flies the trip, not to a brand or a group.
Before the director approves an operator, all of these are in place and saved in the portal:
AOC and aircraft confirmed with the issuing authority or its public register where one exists
Insurance confirmed by the insurer or the operator's insurance broker, not only by a copy, with the amounts in 8.2
IS-BAO registration, or a completed Archē operator questionnaire on safety management, crew training and maintenance
A review of the operator's safety documents (safety management manual, training and maintenance records), with a visit to the operator where practical
No adverse history in public accident databases in the last five years
Two references from brokers or clients who have flown with the operator

The operator's written commitment that every crew flying our trips meets the crew minimums: captain at least 3,000 hours in total and 250 hours on the type; first officer at least 1,000 hours in total

For every trip with an approved operator, the per-trip checks in 8.2 still apply: the aircraft on the AOC, insurance current, two pilots on jets, history clear, not suspended, and the approval valid on the date of the last flight.

An approval ends at once, before the twelve months are up, if the operator has an accident or serious incident (it is suspended, 8.2), its insurance lapses or falls below the minimum, its AOC changes or is suspended, or it fails sanctions screening. The director can withdraw an approval at any time. A renewal needs the checks again.

An operator that is neither audited (8.2) nor approved can be used only with the director's approval for that one trip, after the same checks. If we expect to use it again, approve it for twelve months instead.

Every quote and charter confirmation states the operator's safety status in one line, so the client always knows: the audit and its expiry date (for example "ARGUS Platinum, valid to 30 June 2027"), "Archē-approved operator, approval valid to …", or "Approved by the director for this trip". The portal writes this line from the Operator safety record.

ARGUS Gold Plus no longer exists. ARGUS Gold Certified is described by ARGUS as a remote, one-day audit, so it does not replace the on-site audit that Gold Plus required (ARGUS, 30 April 2026). The standard in 8.2 keeps an independent audit of the operator: on site for ARGUS Platinum and WYVERN Wingman, by a third-party auditor for IS-BAO. An Archē approval is our own review and is described to clients as exactly that.

8.5 Crew and insurance

Ask the operator to confirm in writing two pilots on every jet flight, and that the crew are type-rated and current on the aircraft; on long-range trips, ask about their experience on the type and route. A single-pilot jet flight stops the trip.

Insurance must cover commercial passenger flights, with passenger liability of at least USD 50 million for jets and USD 25 million for turboprops. In the United States, cover of USD 50 to 100 million is typical for turbojets (NBAA, 2024). Record the amount in the portal; a lower amount stops the trip.

Archē carries no liability insurance of its own in its first months: all aircraft, passenger and third-party cover is the operator's. So on every trip check the certificate: the amount, valid on every flight date, the aircraft registration on it, the route inside its territorial cover, and confirmed with the insurer or the operator's insurance broker (once per certificate; the operator library keeps it for the next trip). A gap stops the trip.
Where possible, ask the operator to add the client, and Archē, as additional insured on its policy.
Check the regulator's public records for enforcement action against the operator where they exist.

9.2 Costs that cannot be fixed before the flight

Some costs depend on the day: de-icing, extra parking or hangar time, extra crew nights after a schedule change, late catering, Wi-Fi data use, changing airport or passenger taxes, and permit fees for late changes. Treat them the same way every time:
Never put a number on them unless the operator or supplier has given it in writing.
List them in the quote and in Part A of the confirmation as "at cost, invoiced after the flight with receipts".
If the client asks how much, ask the operator for its best estimate in writing and pass it on as the operator's estimate, never as a fixed price.
After the flight, recharge only what the operator invoices, with receipts, with no margin unless the confirmation says otherwise.
